# Changing a table's shape

The six verbs work down a table. Sometimes the table is the wrong shape to
begin with: a year in four columns when you wanted a year in four rows, or the
reverse.

The target shape has a name and a paper of its own. A table is *tidy* when
each variable is a column and each observation is a row [@wickham2014tidy],
and most of what a pipeline can do, it can only do to a table in that shape.
Real tables arrive the other way as often as not, because the shape that is
easy to type into is rarely the shape that is easy to ask questions of.

Two verbs turn a table one way and back, and the names say which. `lengthen`
makes it taller and `widen` makes it wider, because nobody could remember
which of `melt` and `cast` did what, and a verb whose direction is not in its
name has to be looked up every time. `lengthen` comes first in this part
because it is the direction data usually needs on arrival; `widen` is the way
back, for the table a person reads rather than the table a pipeline works on.

One law holds the part together: **the same facts, either shape**. Reshaping
moves values, and it never invents or discards one; where a verb has to
decide something you did not say, it prints the assumption back, so what it
chose is on the page rather than in your imagination. A reader arriving from
tidyr will recognize the job here and not the argument list, and the first
chapter has a table comparing the two.
